props.title: Fahrenheit 9/11
props.initialSlug: The truth will set you free.

sections.content: Michael Moore's explosive Fahrenheit 9/11 revolutionized political documentary filmmaking while becoming the highest-grossing documentary of all time. Moore weaponized dark humor and damning footage to criticize the Bush administration's response to 9/11 and the subsequent Iraq War. The film's confrontational style influenced a wave of political docs like An Inconvenient Truth (2006) and Inside Job (2010). While critics accused Moore of cherry-picking facts, his provocative approach transformed documentaries from dry educational pieces into mainstream entertainment with bite.

sections.content: The post-9/11 documentary landscape exploded with urgent political filmmaking. The World Trade Center: Rise and Fall of an American Icon (2002) provided immediate historical context, while 9/11 (2002) by the Naudet brothers offered accidental front-line footage of that day. Military documentaries like Gunner Palace (2004) and The War Tapes (2006) embedded with troops in Iraq, providing raw, unfiltered perspectives from the ground.

Moore's techniques - combining archival footage, personal narrative, and confrontational interviews - influenced countless documentarians. Iraq for Sale (2006) exposed war profiteering, The Ground Truth (2006) highlighted veterans' struggles, and Standard Operating Procedure (2008) investigated Abu Ghraib. These films shared Moore's anger while developing their own distinct voices. SUBHEAD: Impact on Modern Documentary Filmmaking

sections.content: Moore's success emboldened documentarians to tackle controversial subjects head-on. Inside Job (2010) used similar techniques to expose Wall Street corruption, while Citizenfour (2014) provided a thrilling real-time look at Edward Snowden's NSA revelations. The rise of streaming platforms has further democratized political documentaries, with films like The Great Hack (2019) and The Social Dilemma (2020) reaching global audiences instantly.
